english: Moreover, for the sake of one piece of jade to court the displeasure of mighty Qin is not right.
So the King of Zhao fasted five days, had me bear the jade, and solemnly sent the letter of gift in the courtyard.
Why? To honour the majesty of a great state and show due reverence.
Now I have come, yet Your Majesty sees me only in a common hall, the courtesy most arrogant;
you got the jade and passed it among your beauty-maids, to make sport of me.
If Your Majesty must press me hard, my head and the jade shall be dashed together on the pillar this instant!
When the King of Zhao sent the jade, he fasted five days; now Your Majesty too should fast five days and set the Nine Guests in the court—only then will I dare present the jade.
After the King of Qin had fasted five days, he set the Nine Guests ceremony in the court and summoned the envoy of Zhao, Lin Xiangru.
I truly feared to be deceived by Your Majesty and to fail Zhao, so I had a man carry the jade back, and it has already reached Zhao by a secret way.
Now, with Qin's might, if you first cut fifteen cities and give them to Zhao, would Zhao dare keep the jade and offend Your Majesty?

Some attendants wished to drag Xiangru away, but the King of Qin said: "To kill Xiangru now would still not gain the jade, and would sever the friendship of Qin and Zhao; better to treat him generously on that account and send him back to Zhao. Would the King of Zhao deceive Qin for the sake of one piece of jade!"
After Xiangru returned, the King of Zhao, judging him a worthy minister who had not disgraced his mission among the lords, appointed him Grand Minister.
Later Qin attacked Zhao and took Shicheng.
The King of Qin sent an envoy to the King of Zhao wishing to hold a friendly meeting at Mianchi, west of the West River.
The King of Zhao feared Qin and wished not to go.
So he met the King of Qin at Mianchi.
Lin Xiangru came forward and said: "I have privately heard that the King of Qin excels in the music of Qin; may I present this basin to Your Majesty for mutual entertainment?"
The King of Qin refused to strike the basin.
Xiangru said: "Within five paces, I beg to spatter Your Majesty with the blood of my neck!"
Thereupon the King of Qin, unwilling, struck the basin once.
Xiangru turned and summoned the historian of Zhao to write: "On such a year, month and day, the King of Qin struck the basin for the King of Zhao."
When the feast ended, the King of Qin could not in the end gain the upper hand over Zhao.
Thereupon the retainers together remonstrated: "The reason we left our kin to serve you is that we admire your lofty righteousness.

Now you and Lian Po hold equal rank; Lord Lian spreads ugly words and you cower and hide from him—your fear is extreme. Even a common man would be ashamed of this, how much more a general and minister!"
The reason I act thus is to put the state's peril first and private grudges last.
In the end they became friends again, neck-cutting friends.
A mountain need not be high—if an immortal dwells there, it is famed.
Water need not be deep—if a dragon dwells there, it is numinous.
This is a humble room, but my virtue makes it fragrant.
Moss stains climb the steps, greening them; grass colour enters the bamboo blinds.
In talk and laughter are learned men; coming and going, none unlettered.
One may tune the unadorned zither and read the gilded scriptures.
No strings and flutes to din the ear, no documents to toil the frame.
Zhuge's cottage of Nanyang, Ziyun's pavilion of Western Shu.
Confucius said: "What crudeness is there?"
Of flowers on land and water, of grasses and trees, the lovely ones are many.
Tao Yuanming of Jin alone loved chrysanthemums.
Since the Tang, the world has greatly loved the peony.

I alone love the lotus, rising from mud yet unstained, bathed in clear ripples yet not coquettish; hollow within and straight without, neither creeping nor branching, its fragrance the farther the purer, standing tall and clean—one may gaze at it from afar, but not toy with it.
To me, the chrysanthemum is the recluse among flowers;
the peony, the man of wealth and rank among flowers;
the lotus, the gentleman among flowers.
For love of the chrysanthemum, after Tao it was seldom heard of.
For love of the lotus, who is of one mind with me?
For love of the peony—fitting indeed that it be many!
Through the seven hundred li of the Three Gorges, ranges link on both banks with never a gap.
Rock upon rock, cliff upon cliff, they veil the sky and screen the sun.
Unless at noon or midnight, neither sun nor moon is seen.
In summer the waters swell to the hills, blocking both down and upstream passage.

When the sovereign's orders must be sped, one sometimes leaves Baidi at dawn and reaches Jiangling by dusk—a thousand two hundred li between; even riding a galloping horse or the wind were not swifter.
In spring and winter, white rapids and green pools whirl with mirrored reflections.
On sheer peaks grow strange cypresses; hanging springs and waterfalls rush and splash among them—clear, swift, steep, lush, a wealth of delight.
On the night of the twelfth of the tenth month of the sixth year of Yuanfeng, I undressed for sleep as moonlight entered the door; gladly I rose and walked.
Bethinking myself of none to share the joy, I went to Chengtian Temple to seek Zhang Huaimin.
Huaimin too was not yet asleep; together we walked in the courtyard.
Beneath the court it was like a pool of limpid water.
In the water waterweeds criss-crossed—they were, in truth, shadows of bamboo and cypress.
What night lacks a moon?
What place lacks bamboo and cypress?
Only there are few idle men like the two of us.
First there is Bo Le, and then there are thousand-li horses.
Thousand-li horses are common, but Bo Le is not.
Hence, though there be famous steeds, they are only dishonoured in the hands of stablemen, dying in pairs between stable and trough, never named as thousand-li horses.
A horse of a thousand li may eat at one feed a whole dan of millet.
But the groom, not knowing it can run a thousand li, feeds it as an ordinary horse.
Such a horse, though having thousand-li powers, eats unfilled, lacks strength, its talents and beauty unseen abroad; unable even to equal a common horse, how ask it to run a thousand li?
Driven not by the right method, fed not to its full capacity, whistled at yet not understood—standing there with whip in hand, he says: "No good horse in the world!"
Alas! Is it truly that there are no horses?
Truly he does not know horses!
